mainTopic: Joint ventures and partners, a tenant's duties to the field, and measuring a 'pile' and inferior olives
overview: The amud opens by finishing a rule: two ventures written in one שטר are counted together, which works against the manager. רבא then rules that a manager who quietly covered a loss cannot later ask the investor to share it. He also rules that when two partners run a venture together, one cannot force a split, even if he offers to keep sharing losses. Next, a משנה rules that a tenant farmer must weed the field. The גמרא explains that weed seeds already in the soil will keep growing after he leaves. A second משנה rules that a tenant must keep working a weak field if it yields enough for a pile. The גמרא then defines how big a pile is: a shovel buried in the grain, or a set amount of two or three סאה. The amud ends by explaining פריצי זיתים, 'wicked' olives that give little oil, and by measuring how little oil that means.

steps.title: Two ventures written in one document
steps.stepSummary: If two ventures are written in one שטר, they are counted together. Any loss falls on the לוה (the manager).
steps.simpleTranslation: Two ventures and one document: the loss is on the borrower.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a rule that started just before. It explains what happens when two ventures are recorded in a single document.
steps.deeperAnalysis: With one שטר, the two ventures are treated as one account. So profit from one venture covers loss in the other. The manager cannot hand a loss on one venture to the investor while keeping the profit from the other.

keyTerms.meaning: A business venture where one person gives money or goods and another trades with it
Borrower; here, the manager who received the venture money

phrases.english: Two joint ventures and one document
the loss is the borrower's.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the contrast with the previous case of two ventures in two documents
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Two ventures in one שטר are counted together, which works against the manager.

steps.title: A manager who quietly covered a loss
steps.stepSummary: A manager lost money, covered the loss himself, and did not tell the investor. רבא rules he cannot later ask the investor to share that loss.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Someone took a venture from his friend and lost money. He worked to fill the gap and did not tell him. He cannot say, 'Share that loss with me.' The investor can answer: 'You filled it so people would not call you a loser of ventures.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new ruling about a manager who covered a loss in secret. He also gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The manager's silence shows he paid for his own reasons, to protect his good name. He was not lending money to the venture. So the investor can say the money was the manager's own choice, and he owes nothing back.

keyTerms.meaning: He made an effort and filled it up (covered the loss)
Carry / bear (a share of the loss)
Someone who loses ventures (a bad business reputation)

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that keeping quiet about a payment can show the payment was meant for oneself, so it cannot be claimed back later.

phrases.english: And Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דְּקַבֵּיל עִיסְקָא מִן חַבְרֵיהּ
phrases.english: This one who receives a joint venture from his fellow
and lost money,
made an effort and filled up the loss
and did not inform him,
he cannot say to him:
Bear that loss together with me.
Because the investor can say to him:
This is why you made the effort and filled it up:
phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets; the corrected wording uses the word in square brackets instead.

phrases.aramaic: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא לִיקְרוֹ לָךְ ״מַפְסֵיד עִיסְקֵי״.
phrases.english: so that they would not call you a "loser of ventures."

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הַאי מַאן דְּקַבֵּיל עִיסְקָא מִן חַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new, separate ruling of רבא about עיסקא
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A manager who quietly covered a loss cannot later ask the investor to share it, because he did it to protect his reputation.

steps.title: One partner wants to divide the profits and end the venture
steps.stepSummary: Two managers made a profit together. If one wants to divide and stop, the other can block him by saying, 'Let us earn more.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: Two people ran a venture together and made a profit. One said, 'Come, let us divide.' If the other says, 'Let us earn more,' the law is that he can hold it back.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא opens a new ruling about two partners running a venture. This is the first of four requests to split. Each later request is more modest or more generous than the one before, yet the other partner can still refuse every one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The partner who wants to keep going wins. Ending the venture early would take away his chance to earn more profit.

keyTerms.meaning: The law is that he can hold it back

phrases.english: And Rava said:

phrases.aramaic: הָנֵי בֵּי תְרֵי דְּעָבְדִי עִיסְקָא בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
phrases.english: These two who run a joint venture together
and made a profit,
and one said to his fellow:
Come, let us divide,
if the other says to him:
Let us profit more,
the law is that he can hold it back.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רָבָא: הָנֵי בֵּי תְרֵי דְּעָבְדִי עִיסְקָא בַּהֲדֵי הֲדָדֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new ruling of רבא, about two partners instead of a manager and an investor
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One partner cannot force the venture to end if the other wants to keep earning.

steps.title: Asking for just half the profit
steps.stepSummary: The partner now asks only for his half of the profit. The other answers that the profit is tied to the principal.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he said, 'Give me half the profit,' the other can say, 'The profit is tied to the principal.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is a smaller request than ending the whole venture. רבא shows that the other partner can still refuse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The profit and the קרן (principal) work together as one fund. Taking out profit makes the fund smaller, so the venture can earn less. That is why the other partner does not have to agree.

phrases.english: And if he said to him:
Give me half of the profit,
he can say to him:
The profit is tied to the principal.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמַר לֵיהּ: הַב לִי פַּלְגָא דְּרַוְוחָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from ending the whole venture to asking only for half the profit
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A partner cannot pull out his share of the profit, because the profit stays tied to the principal.

steps.title: Asking for half the profit and half the principal
steps.stepSummary: The partner asks for half of everything, profit and principal. The other answers that the whole venture is bound to both of them.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he said, 'Give me half the profit and half the principal,' the other can say, 'The venture is bound to both of us.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new version of the request: split everything evenly. Again רבא lets the other partner refuse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even a fair, even split is refused. The venture was taken on by both of them together, so neither one can take it apart alone.

keyTerms.meaning: The venture is bound to both partners together

phrases.english: And if he said to him:

phrases.aramaic: הַב לִי פַּלְגָא רַוְוחָא וּפַלְגָא קַרְנָא –
phrases.english: Give me half the profit and half the principal,
he can say to him:
The venture is bound to both of us.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמַר לֵיהּ: הַב לִי פַּלְגָא רַוְוחָא וּפַלְגָא קַרְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens the request from half the profit to half of everything
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A partner cannot force an even split of profit and principal, because the venture is bound to both partners.

steps.title: Even promising to share losses does not force a split
steps.stepSummary: The partner offers to split everything and still share any future loss. The other can refuse, because two people together have better luck.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if he said, 'Let us divide the profit and divide the principal, and if you have a loss I will share it with you,' the other can say, 'No. The luck of two is better.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the strongest offer, since the partner promises to keep sharing losses. רבא still lets the other partner refuse.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The promise to share losses answers the money worry from before. But the other partner has another reason to stay together: two partners have better מזל than one. So in every one of these cases, the partner who wants to keep the venture going wins.

keyTerms.meaning: I will bear (the loss) with you

steps.whatToRemember: In a venture run by two partners, one cannot force a split of profit, of principal, or of both, even if he promises to share losses. The partner who wants to continue can always hold the venture together.

phrases.english: And if he said to him:
Let us divide the profit and divide the principal,
and if a loss reaches you
I will bear it with you,
he can say to him: No,
the luck of two is better.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמַר לֵיהּ: נִפְלוֹג רַוְוחָא וְנִפְלוֹג קַרְנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The last and strongest offer to split, which is still refused
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even with a promise to share losses, one partner cannot force a split, because the luck of two is better.

steps.title: A tenant may not refuse to weed the field
steps.stepSummary: The משנה rules that a tenant who pays fixed rent cannot skip weeding, because weeds will hurt the field after he leaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone rents a field from his friend and does not want to weed it, and says, 'Why do you care? I am paying you your rent anyway,' we do not listen to him. The owner can say: 'Tomorrow you will leave this field, and it will grow weeds for me.'
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It rules that a tenant must weed the field even though his rent stays the same either way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tenant argues that the owner loses nothing, since the rent is fixed. The משנה rejects this. The owner cares about the field's future, not only this year's rent.

keyTerms.meaning: The משנה, the base text the גמרא discusses
One who takes a field from its owner to farm it
Your fixed rent, paid in produce
We do not listen to him; his claim is rejected

steps.whyThisMatters: It teaches that a renter must protect the owner's property for the long term, not only pay what he owes.

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who receives a field from his fellow
and did not want to weed it,
and he said to him: What do you care?

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וַאֲנִי נוֹתֵן לְךָ אֶת חֲכִירָךְ –
phrases.english: Since I am giving you your rent
phrases.notes: This tenant pays a set amount of produce each year, no matter how the crop turns out.

phrases.english: we do not listen to him.
Because the owner can say to him:
Tomorrow you will leave it,
and it will grow weeds for me.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמְקַבֵּל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ וְלֹא רָצָה לְנַכֵּשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה about tenant farmers, after the earlier discussion of business managers.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tenant cannot refuse to weed, even with fixed rent, because the weeds will hurt the owner's field in later years.

steps.title: Offer one: I will plow out the weeds after harvest
steps.stepSummary: The tenant offers to plow the weeds out later. The owner answers that he wants top-quality wheat.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the tenant says, 'After the harvest I will plow the field and clear the weeds,' the owner can answer: 'I want high-quality wheat.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a list of offers the tenant might make, with the owner's answer to each. This is the first offer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Plowing later would fix the field for the future. The owner still has a complaint about this year's crop: wheat that grows among weeds is weaker.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה

phrases.english: GEMARA: If he says to him:
Afterward I will plow it,
phrases.notes: He means after the harvest, plowing the field to pull up the weeds.

phrases.english: he can say to him: I want top-quality wheat.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts testing the משנה's ruling against offers the tenant might make.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Plowing later is not enough, because the owner wants good wheat this year.

steps.title: Offer two: I will buy you wheat at the market
steps.stepSummary: The tenant offers to buy good wheat elsewhere. The owner answers that he wants wheat from his own land.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the tenant says, 'I will buy you good wheat from the market,' the owner can answer: 'I want wheat from my own land.'
steps.whatsHappening: The second offer: the tenant will replace the weaker wheat with good wheat from the market.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answers the owner's complaint about quality. The owner still refuses, because he has a right to produce grown on his own field.

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמַר לֵיהּ: זָבֵינְנָא לָךְ חִטֵּי מִשּׁוּקָא –
phrases.english: And if he says to him: I will buy you wheat from the market,
he can say to him: I want wheat from my land.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמַר לֵיהּ: זָבֵינְנָא לָךְ חִטֵּי מִשּׁוּקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The tenant raises a better offer that answers the owner's previous complaint.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Market wheat is not enough, because the owner wants wheat from his own field.

steps.title: Offer three: I will weed only your share
steps.stepSummary: The tenant offers to weed only enough for the owner's portion. The owner answers that a half-weedy field gives his land a bad name.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the tenant says, 'I will weed only the amount that covers your share,' the owner can answer: 'You are giving my land a bad name.'
steps.whatsHappening: The third offer: the tenant will weed only the part that produces the owner's rent.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the owner gets good wheat from his own land. He still objects, because people who see a field full of weeds will think his land is poor.

keyTerms.meaning: A bad name, a bad reputation

phrases.english: And if he says to him: I will weed for you
the amount of your share,

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ: קָא מַנְסְבַתְּ שֵׁם רַע לְאַרְעַאי.
phrases.english: he can say to him: You are giving my land a bad name.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמַר לֵיהּ מְנַכֵּישְׁנָא לָךְ שִׁיעוּר מְנָתָיךְ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The tenant makes his final offer, and the owner gives a new reason to refuse.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Partial weeding is not enough, because a weedy field hurts the land's reputation.

steps.title: But the משנה gives a different reason
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the משנה's reason is weeds in the future. That does not fit the owner's first reply, 'I want top-quality wheat,' which is about this year's crop.
steps.simpleTranslation: But we learned in the משנה that the reason is: 'Because it will grow weeds for me!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the owner's reply to the first offer (step 8). The משנה named future weeds as the reason, not the quality of this year's wheat.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tenant offered to plow the weeds out after the harvest. The answer 'I want top-quality wheat' is about this year's crop, but the משנה's reason is about the field after the tenant leaves. So the owner's reply to that offer has to be about future weeds.

phrases.english: But didn't we learn:
Because it will grow weeds for me!
phrases.notes: This is quoting the end of the משנה from step 7.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the owner's reply in step 8 because it does not match the משנה's stated reason of future weeds.
steps.kashyaTarget: The owner's reply to the first offer in step 8: 'I want top-quality wheat.'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה gives future weeds as the only reason, so the owner's real argument must be about future weeds.

steps.title: The seed that fell has fallen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the owner's reply is that weed seeds already dropped into the soil will keep growing, even after plowing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the reason is that the owner can say to him: 'The seed that fell has fallen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new answer that fits the משנה's words. Plowing later does not help, because the weed seeds are already in the ground.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answers the tenant's first offer, 'I will plow afterward.' Even if he pulls up the weeds, their seeds have dropped into the soil and will sprout in later years. That is exactly the משנה's reason: the field will grow weeds after the tenant leaves.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather (drops the earlier explanation for a new one)
That fell has fallen; it is already done

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה's reason is about the future: weed seeds that drop into the soil keep growing for years, so plowing later cannot fix the harm.

phrases.english: Rather, it is because he can say to him:
The seed that fell has fallen.
phrases.notes: He means the weeds have already dropped their seeds into the soil, and plowing can't take them back out.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא מִשּׁוּם דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ: בִּזְרָא דִּנְפַל – נְפַל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11 with a reason that matches the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Replaces the earlier explanation with one that fits the משנה's wording
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The owner rejects the offer to plow later because he wants good wheat this year.
steps.terutzMaskana: The owner rejects plowing later because the weed seeds already in the soil will grow in future years.

steps.title: A field with a poor crop must still be harvested
steps.stepSummary: A new משנה rules that if a rented field produced little, the tenant must still tend it as long as it yields enough for a pile.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone rents a field from his friend and it did not produce much, then if it has enough to make a pile of grain, he must still take care of it.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה opens. It covers a field that produced so little that working it is barely worth the effort.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The tenant might want to give up on a weak crop. The משנה sets a minimum: if there is enough for a pile, he must keep working it and give the owner his share.

keyTerms.meaning: To take care of it, keep working it

phrases.english: MISHNA: One who receives a field from his fellow
and it did not produce much,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ בָּהּ כְּדֵי לְהַעֲמִיד כְּרִי –
phrases.english: if it has enough to form a pile,
he is obligated to take care of it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ הַמְקַבֵּל שָׂדֶה מֵחֲבֵירוֹ וְלֹא עָשְׂתָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה about a different problem with a rented field.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: If the weak crop is enough to form a pile, the tenant must keep working the field.

steps.title: רבי יהודה: the measure is the amount of seed sown
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה says a pile is not a fixed size, so the real test is whether the crop equals the seed that was planted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה said: What kind of fixed measure is a pile? Rather, the test is whether the field has as much as the seed that was sown in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה disagrees with the measure the first opinion in the משנה gave. He offers a different minimum.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A pile can be big or small, so it is not a clear standard. רבי יהודה ties the minimum to the field itself: if the crop equals the seed that was planted, the tenant must keep working it.

keyTerms.meaning: The amount of seed sown in the field

steps.whatToRemember: The first opinion sets the minimum at enough for a pile. רבי יהודה sets it at the amount of seed that was planted.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda said:
What fixed measure is there in a pile?

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא אִם יֵשׁ בָּהּ כְּדֵי נְפִילָה.
phrases.english: Rather, the test is whether it has the amount that was dropped.
phrases.notes: 'Dropped' means the seed scattered when the field was planted.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: מַאי קִצְבָה בִּכְרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with the first opinion's measure in step 13 and offers a different one.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The tenant must keep working the field if the crop equals the amount of seed that was sown.

steps.title: The tenant's contract explains why he must keep working
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that a tenant must keep tending a weak field if it can still form a pile, because his contract promises to set up a pile before the owner.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: The חכמים taught: If someone receives a field from his fellow to work, and it did not produce well, then as long as it yields enough to form a pile, he must keep caring for it. This is because he writes in his contract: 'I will start, plow, plant, reap, bind sheaves, thresh, winnow, and set up a pile in front of you. Then you will come and take half, and I will take half for my work and expenses.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins by quoting a ברייתא that repeats the משנה's ruling and adds the reason behind it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new information is the reason. The tenant's own contract lists every stage of farming, ending with 'I will set up a pile before you.' As long as the field can produce a pile, he can still keep his promise, so he must keep working.

keyTerms.meaning: A tenant who works a field for a share of the crop
To take care of, to tend

steps.whyThisMatters: The contract's wording becomes the measure of the tenant's duty. If the field can still make a pile, he can still keep his written promise.

phrases.english: GEMARA
The Sages taught:
One who receives a field from his fellow
and it did not produce,

phrases.aramaic: אִם יֵשׁ בָּהּ כְּדֵי לְהַעֲמִיד כְּרִי –
phrases.english: if it has enough to form a pile,
he is obligated to take care of it.
For this is what he writes to him:
I will stand up, and plow, and plant,
and reap, and bind sheaves, and thresh,
and winnow, and set up a pile before you,
and you will come and take half,
and I, for my work and my expenses, half.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה from step 13 by supplying the reason for its ruling.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A tenant must tend a weak field if it can form a pile, because his contract promises to set up a pile before the owner.

steps.title: How big is a pile?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what size counts as 'enough to form a pile.'
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much counts as enough to form a pile?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a measurement. It wants to know how much grain counts as a 'pile.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא and the משנה both depend on the word 'pile' but never give a size. Without a size, nobody knows when the tenant may stop working.

phrases.english: And how much is enough to form a pile in it?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the size of the 'pile' mentioned in the ברייתא.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The minimum size of a כרי.

steps.title: Big enough for a shovel to stand in
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא says a pile is big enough when a winnowing shovel can stand up in it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: Enough grain that a winnowing shovel can stand up in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא answers the question with a practical test: stick the shovel in, and see if it stands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He does not give a number. He gives a physical test instead. If the grain holds the shovel upright without it falling over, that counts as a real pile.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina said:
Enough for the winnowing shovel to stand in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the size question from step 16.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A pile is big enough when a winnowing shovel can stand upright in it.

steps.title: What if the shovel sticks out both sides?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks whether the test still works if the shovel stands but its edges poke out of the pile.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: If the shovel stands up but sticks out from one side of the pile to the other, what is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a follow-up question about the shovel test. The pile holds the shovel up, but the shovel is wider than the pile.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The test 'the shovel stands' leaves a gap. Does the shovel only need to stay upright, or must the grain also cover it? This question looks for the exact limit of the rule.

keyTerms.meaning: It was asked of them; a question raised in the study hall

phrases.english: It was asked of them:

phrases.aramaic: רַחַת הַיּוֹצֵא מֵהַאי גִּיסָא לְהַאי גִּיסָא,
phrases.english: A shovel that sticks out from this side to that side,
what is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the limit of רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא's shovel rule.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether a pile counts when the shovel stands in it but sticks out past its edges.

steps.title: The blade must be fully covered
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבהו reports that רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא himself explained that the shovel's blade must not 'see the sun.' So it must be completely covered.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: רבי אבהו said, 'It was explained to me personally by רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא: it counts whenever the shovel's blade cannot see the face of the sun.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question using a firsthand report from רבי אבהו, who heard the explanation directly from the author of the rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Does not see the sun' means the grain completely buries the blade. A shovel that sticks out on the sides can see the sun, so that pile is not big enough. The question is settled by the rule's own author.

keyTerms.meaning: It was explained to me personally
The blade of the shovel, the part pushed into the grain

phrases.english: Come and hear:
Rabbi Abahu said:
To me it was explained personally
by Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Chanina:
Any pile in which its blade does not
see the face of the sun.
phrases.notes: In other words, the blade is completely buried in the grain, so a shovel sticking out would not count.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the question in step 18 using the original speaker's own explanation.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The blade must be fully covered by grain, so a shovel sticking out does not count.

steps.title: Three סאה or two סאה
steps.stepSummary: Two opinions give the pile a size in numbers: לוי says three סאה, and the school of רבי ינאי says two סאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was stated: לוי says three סאה. The school of רבי ינאי says two סאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a dispute among אמוראים who measure the pile in actual units of volume instead of with the shovel test.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the size of a pile is given as a set number. לוי requires three סאה. The school of רבי ינאי requires only two.

keyTerms.meaning: A measure of volume for grain

phrases.english: It was stated:
Levi says three se'ah;
the school of Rabbi Yannai say two se'ah.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different, number-based answer to the size question from step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A pile is three סאה (לוי) or two סאה (school of רבי ינאי).

steps.title: Two סאה left over after expenses
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש explains that the two סאה are counted after the tenant's expenses are covered.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: The two סאה they spoke about are apart from the expenses.
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש explains the two-סאה opinion. The two סאה must be left over after the costs of farming are paid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Without this explanation, one could think two סאה of total crop is enough. ריש לקיש says the costs come out first, and the field must still leave two סאה beyond that. Only then must the tenant keep working.

keyTerms.meaning: Expenses, the costs of working the field

steps.whatToRemember: A tenant must keep working a weak field if it yields a real pile. That means the shovel's blade is fully buried, or a set amount (three סאה per לוי, or two סאה per the school of רבי ינאי, counted after expenses according to ריש לקיש).

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
The two se'ah that they said
are apart from the expenses.
phrases.notes: He means that after paying the costs, two סאה must still remain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how to count the two סאה from step 20.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The two סאה are counted after expenses, so they are net profit.

steps.title: A new משנה about inferior olives and grapes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes a משנה from elsewhere: בית שמאי say inferior olives and grapes can become impure, and בית הלל say they cannot.
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned in a משנה elsewhere: About poor-quality olives and grapes, בית שמאי say they can become impure, and בית הלל say they cannot.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a משנה from the laws of food impurity. It is setting up a discussion that will come next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question is whether stunted olives and grapes count as food. בית שמאי treat them as food, so they can become impure. בית הלל say they are too poor to count as food, so they cannot.

keyTerms.meaning: We learned there; it quotes a משנה from another place
Poor, stunted fruit that never ripens properly
Rule that it can become ritually impure
Rule that it cannot become ritually impure

steps.confusionAlert: Here מטהרין does not mean the fruit was impure and is now made pure. It means the fruit cannot receive impurity at all, because it does not count as food.

phrases.english: We learned there:
Inferior olives and grapes:
Beit Shammai rule they can become impure,
and Beit Hillel rule they cannot.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the pile measurements and opens a related discussion from the laws of impurity.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Inferior olives and grapes: בית שמאי say they can become impure, and בית הלל say they cannot.

steps.title: What does 'inferior olives' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the meaning of the word פריצי in the phrase פריצי זיתים from the משנה.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are 'פריצי' olives?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops to ask what the unusual word פריצי means in the משנה it just quoted. This question sets up the answers that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה in Step 22 used the word פריצי without explaining it. Before the גמרא can use that משנה, it must first know which olives are meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Inferior or 'unruly' olives (the word under discussion)
What is / what does it mean

phrases.english: What are 'peritzei' olives?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of a word in the משנה quoted in Step 22
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The meaning of the word פריצי

steps.title: רב הונא: they are 'wicked' olives
steps.stepSummary: רב הונא explains that פריצי זיתים means 'wicked olives.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב הונא said: they are wicked olives.
steps.whatsHappening: רב הונא answers the question: פריצי means 'wicked.' These are olives that act 'badly' because they give hardly any oil.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word פריצי is explained as a word for wickedness. Olives that fail to give the oil they should are called 'wicked.'

phrases.english: Rav Huna said:
Wicked olives.
phrases.notes: He means olives that 'misbehave' because they give almost no oil.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 23
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: פריצי means 'wicked': poor olives that give almost no oil

steps.title: רב יוסף finds the word in a פסוק in דניאל
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף supports רב הונא by quoting a פסוק where פריצי means 'wicked people.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף said: what is the פסוק that shows this? 'And the wicked ones (פריצי) of your people will rise up to fulfill the vision, and they will stumble.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף brings a פסוק showing that the word פריצי really does mean 'wicked' in תנ"ך.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא's meaning needs support from how the word is used elsewhere. In the פסוק in דניאל, פריצי clearly describes wicked people, so the same meaning fits the olives.

keyTerms.meaning: And what is the פסוק (that shows this)?

phrases.english: Rav Yosef said:
And what is the verse that shows this?
"And the children of the wicked among your people will raise themselves up
phrases.notes: דניאל 11:14. The word in square brackets is part of the corrected wording.

phrases.english: to establish the vision, but they will stumble."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a פסוק to back up רב הונא's meaning

steps.title: רב נחמן בר יצחק finds the word in a פסוק in יחזקאל
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק brings a different פסוק where פריץ means a violent, wicked person.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: the meaning comes from here: 'And he fathers a son who is a robber (פריץ), a shedder of blood.'
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא offers another פסוק as the source for the same meaning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He agrees with the meaning 'wicked.' He only picks a different פסוק, where פריץ describes a robber who sheds blood.

keyTerms.meaning: A robber or wicked, violent person

phrases.aramaic: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: מֵהָכָא –
phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: from here:
"And he fathers a son who is a robber,
a shedder of blood."

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different פסוק for the same meaning

steps.title: How little oil makes olives 'inferior'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how small the oil yield must be for olives to count as פריצי.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much is 'inferior olives'?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the word is clear, the גמרא asks for a measurement: at what oil amount do olives count as inferior? This sets up the opinions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Wicked olives' is only a description. The גמרא wants a number that tells us exactly when the term applies.

phrases.english: And how much is the amount for inferior olives?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the meaning of the word to its exact measurement
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The oil yield that defines inferior olives

steps.title: Two numbers: four קבין or two סאה per pressing
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says four קבין of oil per pressing; the school of רבי ינאי says two סאה per pressing.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: four קבין per beam. The school of רבי ינאי said: two סאה per beam.
steps.whatsHappening: Two opinions give the measure. If one pressing gives only this much oil, the olives are inferior.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A קורה is the heavy beam of the olive press, so 'per beam' means per pressing. Two סאה equals twelve קבין, so the numbers look very different, three times apart.

keyTerms.meaning: קבין, a small unit of measure (six קבין make one סאה)
The beam of the olive press; one pressing

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says:
Four kav of oil per beam.
phrases.notes: The beam is the press's heavy log, so this means four קבין from one pressing.

phrases.english: The school of Rabbi Yannai say:
Two se'a per beam.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר: אַרְבַּעַת קַבִּין לַקּוֹרָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the measurement question of Step 27 with two opinions
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Four קבין per pressing (רבי אלעזר) or two סאה per pressing (school of רבי ינאי)

steps.title: Not a real argument: it depends how much the press holds
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says the two opinions agree; each is speaking about a place that loads a different amount of olives into the press.
steps.simpleTranslation: They do not disagree. This one is in a place where they load one כור into the press; that one is in a place where they load three כורים into the press.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא shows the two numbers are really the same rule. Each Sage was measuring a press loaded with a different amount of olives.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Where one כור of olives goes in, four קבין of oil marks inferior olives. Where three כורים go in, three times that amount, twelve קבין, which is two סאה, marks inferior olives. The ratio of oil to olives is the same, so there is no real argument.

keyTerms.meaning: A כור, a large measure (thirty סאה)
The basket or press load of olives

steps.whatToRemember: פריצי זיתים are 'wicked' olives that give very little oil. The measure is four קבין of oil for every כור of olives pressed, which matches two סאה when three כורים are pressed.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think רבי אלעזר and the school of רבי ינאי argue about the law. They use the same ratio, just in presses of different sizes.

phrases.english: And they do not disagree:
This is in a place where they bring one kor into the press,
phrases.notes: This is רבי אלעזר's four קבין.

phrases.aramaic: הָא בְּאַתְרָא דִּמְעַיְּילִי תְּלָתָא כּוֹרִין בְּאוֹלָלָא.
phrases.english: and that is in a place where they bring three kor into the press.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Reconciles the two numbers given in Step 28
steps.terutzResolutionType: Different local cases (press size), same underlying ratio
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two Sages argue about how little oil makes olives inferior
steps.terutzMaskana: Both hold four קבין per כור; they just describe presses loaded with one כור or three כורים

steps.title: Opening a new ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins quoting a teaching of the חכמים (a ברייתא).
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught:
steps.whatsHappening: This line only introduces a new ברייתא. The גמרא is setting up the next teaching, which comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: No ruling is given yet. The formula signals that a source from the time of the תנאים is about to be quoted.

phrases.english: The Sages taught:

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Transition: opens a new ברייתא after the discussion of inferior olives closes
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Introductory formula only; the ברייתא's content follows
